stir.label: Stir
stir.effect: Stir with a glass stirring rod to speed up solute dissolution and improve mixing
stir.hint: Stirring accelerates dissolving and heat transfer, and equalizes local concentration so readings represent the bulk solution

shake.label: Shake
shake.effect: Shake to mix thoroughly and ensure full contact between reagents
shake.hint: With small volumes in a test tube, shaking (not stirring) is used to mix — keep the mouth of the tube pointed away from people

heat.label: Heat
heat.effect: Light the alcohol lamp to heat the system and raise its temperature
heat.hint: Most reactions speed up with heat; endothermic reactions require continuous heating to proceed

cool.label: Cool
cool.effect: Remove the heat source and allow the system to cool naturally
cool.hint: Cooling reduces solubility — a standard step for crystallization and product collection

settle.label: Settle
settle.effect: Allow to stand briefly so precipitates sink and liquid layers separate more clearly
settle.hint: Precipitation and phase separation take time; only after settling can you judge whether the supernatant is clear

read.label: Read
read.hint: Read with your eye level with the graduation mark; log each reading in the data table to calculate averages and errors

sodiumLab.largeWarning: A large piece of sodium releases heat violently, which can ignite the hydrogen gas and even cause an explosive pop or splatter of alkali solution. In a real lab, only a mung bean–sized piece may be used. This size is shown here for virtual demonstration only.
sodiumLab.cut: Use a scalpel to cut away the oxidized surface layer
sodiumLab.cutHint: Sodium has a grey-white oxide layer on its surface. Cut a fresh face before placing it in water. After cutting, observe how the sheen of the fresh surface changes.
sodiumLab.phenol: Add 2 drops of phenolphthalein to the water
sodiumLab.drop: Use tweezers to place the sodium into the water
sodiumLab.next: Replace with a fresh cup of water and take a new piece
sodiumLab.burning: The heat ignites the escaping hydrogen gas; sodium burns with a yellow flame
sodiumLab.phenomenaTitle: Phenomena: floats, melts, darts, hisses, turns pink

float.name: Floats on the water surface
float.why: Sodium has a density of 0.97 g/cm³, which is less than water.

melt.name: Melts into a bright, shiny ball
melt.why: The reaction releases heat; sodium's melting point is only 97.8 ℃, so it melts quickly. Surface tension draws it into a sphere.

swim.name: Darts around on the water surface
swim.why: Hydrogen gas jets unevenly from all sides of the ball, propelling it in random directions.

hiss.name: Produces a hissing sound
hiss.why: Hydrogen gas escapes rapidly, and the heat vaporizes the water at the contact point.

pink.name: Solution turns pink
pink.why: The reaction produces the strong base NaOH; phenolphthalein turns pink in the presence of a base. The pink color first appears along the trail left by the sodium ball.

sodiumLab.pinkHint: No phenolphthalein was added, so the alkali produced is not visible. You can add drops now — the base is already in the water.

chart.title: Hydrogen gas volume produced over time
chart.hint: Complete a run to plot the hydrogen production curve here. Try different sodium sizes and compare reaction times.
chart.insight: Sodium reacts only at the surface of the sphere. As the radius shrinks at a constant rate, reaction time is proportional to radius — and therefore to the cube root of mass: an 8× increase in mass yields only ~2× the reaction time.

flameLab.cleanHint: The platinum wire no longer imparts color to the flame and is ready for the next sample.
flameLab.dirtyHint: Residue remains on the platinum wire (new wire often carries sodium). Dip in dilute hydrochloric acid and heat in the flame; repeat until the flame shows no color. The chloride formed volatilizes readily, making this much faster than heating alone.
flameLab.unknownHint: Burn sample X and determine which metal element it contains. Note: the yellow light of sodium can mask the violet light of potassium.
flameLab.wrong: Incorrect. Check whether the platinum wire has been cleaned; if necessary, observe again through cobalt glass.

spectro.title: Spectroscope: Line Spectrum
spectro.empty: Insert the platinum wire dipped in a sample into the flame to display its spectrum here.
spectro.explain: Each element emits light at only a few fixed wavelengths, like a fingerprint. Sodium produces a pair of yellow lines at 589 nm; potassium's main lines are at 766 nm (deep red) and 404 nm (violet), giving potassium flames a pale violet color. Cobalt glass absorbs the yellow-green light in between, transmitting only the two ends.

clockLab.starch: Add starch indicator to Solution A
clockLab.pour: Pour in Solution B and start timer
clockLab.excessThio: Na₂S₂O₃ is at least twice H₂O₂: any iodine formed is immediately reduced back — the solution will never turn blue.
clockLab.overdue: No color change after 5 minutes. Check the recipe, or press “Stop timing” to end this run.
clockLab.noStarch: No starch present — the endpoint can only be detected when enough iodine accumulates to show a yellow-brown color, so the recorded time will be longer than expected.

chart.title: Data analysis: reaction order and activation energy
chart.order: Fitted slope ≈ {n}, giving a reaction order of {n} with respect to I⁻ (theoretical: 1st order)
chart.orderHint: Keep temperature, H₂O₂, and Na₂S₂O₃ constant; vary only the KI concentration across at least two runs to determine the reaction order with respect to I⁻.
chart.ea: Activation energy derived from slope −Ea/R: Ea ≈ {ea} kJ/mol (literature value ≈ 56 kJ/mol)
chart.eaHint: Keep the recipe constant; vary only the temperature across at least two runs and apply the Arrhenius equation to determine the activation energy.
